newsitem.title: USA: U.S. debt futures end steady, showing resilience.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debt futures end steady, showing resilience.

text.p: U.S. debt futures ended unchanged after a low-volume session marked by resilience in the face of a 28-year high in U.S. consumer confidence and a mediocre two-year note sale.

September bond futures dipped to session lows midmorning following news that U.S. consumer confidence rose to a 28-year high, but managed to claw back up and hover close to the 112-00 level for the rest of the session.
Even the arrival of $15.5 billion in new two-year Treasury notes, which capped the market on the upside, ultimately had little impact on prices, traders and analysts said.

"The fact that the market managed to push higher today speaks volumes for the overall upbeat mood people are in regarding the uptrend in the market near term," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist for First Chicago Capital Markets.

Bond futures have been trending in an upward channel since April. Traders and analysts said widespread expectations for the Federal Reserve to remain on hold at its two-day policy meeting next week are the behind the market's resiliency.
"Nobody in the world believes the Fed is going to raise rates," Karydakis said.
This morning, the Conference Board said its confidence index climbed to 129.6 in June from a revised 127.9 in May, and its senior economist predicted it could rise further.
Analysts characterized Treasury's two-year note sale at midday as unimpressive but in line with expectations, which helped explain why futures showed little reaction to the results.

The two-year note was awarded at 6.027 percent, compared with a yield of 6.02 percent in when-issued trading just prior to the auction. The bid-to-cover ratio was 2.46, with non-competitive tenders at $1.15 billion.

The Treasury market also seemed to recover quickly from a case of nerves on Monday when Japanese Prime Minister Hashimoto said Japan might be tempted to sell its U.S. Treasury holdings if the dollar fell sharply. Debt futures traders deemed such a scenario highly implausible, and Japan's Finance Ministry later said Hashimoto's comments had been misinterpreted.

On Wednesday, U.S. durable goods orders for May will be reported at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT, and bond traders said any outsized number could rattle the market anew. Orders are seen rising by 0.6 percent following a 1.3 percent gain in April. At midday, Treasury will auction $11.5 billion in five-year notes.
A Eurodollar futures trader said the market was already gearing for next week, when a bevy of potentially market-moving factors are packed into a 3-1/2-day workweek.
He predicted futures would see more low-volume trading this week and mild price pressure as longs trim back their holdings before the two-day Fed meeting and June employment report.
"Next week is such a huge week that you can't expect anything to happen this week," he said.

September bond futures ended unchanged at at 112-5/32, December Eurodollars were unchanged at 93.94, and September 10-year note futures were also unchanged at 108-17/32. ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750)) E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
